attendees.role: presenter, Comprehensive Environmental (storm water utility fee consultant)

budget_items.what_was_said: The task force asked why the most recent data showed 17 large-area properties subject to the fee versus 21 in earlier data; the consultant said some properties turned out not to be subject to the ERU fee.

budget_items.topic: Parcels subject to the ERU fee
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant said about 543 parcels have been identified as subject to an ERU-based fee, excluding residential, town-owned, and no-impervious-area parcels.

budget_items.topic: Original memo property count vs. new count
budget_items.what_was_said: A member noted the original memo cited roughly 4,800 properties, which the consultant clarified excludes residential and town-owned parcels.

budget_items.topic: Proposed ERU tier and fee structure
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant proposed expanding ERU tiers so tier one pays $60 per equivalent unit and a new top tier covers 200 or more units, to reduce the revenue gap.
One equivalent residential unit was defined as 4,200 square feet of impervious area, the basis for all tier calculations.

The DPW director's draft budget for the program, after removing Chapter 90 and one-time purchases, was cited at several figures before the group settled on roughly 873 as the revenue target for fee-setting.

budget_items.topic: Capital project money within the draft budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The draft budget included $300,000 a year for stormwater projects, though the DPW director said current annual project spending is less than $100,000 due to staff and funding limits.

budget_items.topic: Indirect costs in the utility budget
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director modeled about $10,000 in indirect/administrative costs into the utility budget, patterned on the sewer enterprise fund.

budget_items.topic: New staff positions funded by the utility
budget_items.what_was_said: The DPW director confirmed the plan involves three new hires, including a dedicated stormwater equipment operator and a GIS engineer, funded through the proposed utility rather than the operating budget.

The consultant suggested a cutoff (e.g. 100 square feet) below which small residential impervious areas would not be billed, which would remove about 80 properties and roughly $4,800 from the fee schedule.
A property near Lunenburg/Shirley previously listed with minimal impervious area was found to have close to 19 acres (roughly 800,000 square feet), prompting talk of adding higher fee tiers.

budget_items.topic: Correction to the large-property ERU estimate
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant corrected her earlier figure, saying the large property is closer to 197-199 equivalent residential units, just under the proposed 200-unit top tier.

The consultant's data showed about 580 acres of right-of-way parcels, mostly one large parcel, while the DPW director's own pavement survey put town-owned roads at 238 acres, differing from an earlier-cited figure of 383 acres.
A member noted potential fines of up to $50,000 per day for MS4 noncompliance, though nobody could confirm any town had actually been fined.

budget_items.topic: Estimated ERU fee for the Walmart/Mass Ave property
budget_items.what_was_said: The consultant's spreadsheet showed the Walmart-area commercial parcel at roughly 202 equivalent residential units, which a member questioned as seeming low for the size of the property.

decisions.decision: Task force will ask the assessor's office (Linda McQuade) for a list of parcels newly built or occupied since 2016 to help cross-reference impervious-area changes.
Task force will pursue expanding ERU fee tiers beyond the current tier 10 to capture very large properties like the ~19-acre site.
Sarah Dewal (Comprehensive Environmental) will send the task force an updated parcel spreadsheet and the presentation slides by the next day.
Next meeting set for September 25th rather than the usual third Thursday, due to a member's unavailability.
Task force will try to set up a conversation with 'Jen' about the cost of hiring a dedicated consultant for the utility rollout.

minutes.headline: Task force stalled on a stormwater utility fee because the underlying impervious-area data is a decade out of date
minutes.summary:
The Stormwater Task Force reviewed a consultant's answers to prior questions and discovered the state's impervious-area GIS data underlying its proposed fee structure has not been updated since 2016, undercounting many developed and expanded properties. The group discussed revising ERU fee tiers, weighed funding the work through a dedicated utility versus the DPW's operating budget, and decided to seek updated parcel data from the assessor's office before setting any fee, with the next meeting tentatively set for September 25th.</parameter>
</invoke>

what_happened.line: The task force found the state's impervious-area GIS data behind its proposed stormwater fee has not been updated since 2016, undercounting developed properties.
Members agreed to ask the assessor's office for parcels built or occupied since 2016 before any fee is set.
The consultant proposed adding higher ERU fee tiers after a roughly 19-acre property was found to have far more impervious area than earlier data showed.
The group weighed funding the stormwater program through a dedicated utility fee versus the DPW's operating budget, citing exposure to state MS4 fines if funding lapses.
The next meeting was moved to September 25th instead of the usual third Thursday.

why_it_matters: A new stormwater utility fee, billed by impervious surface area, is still under design and has not been set; any property owner could eventually see a line item tied to how much pavement or roof area they have.
The fee structure depends on parcel data the task force says is out of date, so which properties and how much they would owe is not yet settled.
How the stormwater program is funded -- a dedicated fee versus the town's existing operating budget -- will affect whether it appears as a new charge or as part of general tax-funded services.
